docs.title: The Wave Function
docs.text:
In quantum mechanics, the state of an isolated system is described by its wave function, denoted by the Greek letter \(\Psi\).

The time-dependent Schrödinger equation governs how this wave function evolves over time:

\[i\hbar\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\Psi(\mathbf{r},t)=\hat{H}\Psi(\mathbf{r},t)\]

Notice how the inline math like \(\hbar\) fits perfectly into the text, while the block equation stands out on its own.

docs.title: 0.1 Introduction to the Lecture
docs.text:
This is a lecture note written from the 2026 International Summer School for Advanced Undergraduate Students, which is held at KAIST, Daejeon.

This lecture, Curve Shortening Flow, was given by Professor Beomjun Choi, KAIST. His research interest lies in the intersection of differential geometry and partial differential equations. The subject of curve shortening flow is one of the premier topics residing precisely in this intersection.

We will omit some foundational knowledge of PDEs during this lecture, as explaining the full rigorous theory of partial differential equations would take several semesters.

Before we introduce our main topic, the curve shortening flow, we will briefly dive into the basic notion of the heat equation.

docs.title: 0.2 Heat Equation
docs.text:
Consider a function \(u(\theta, t)\), where \(\theta \in S^1 = \mathbb{R} / 2\pi \mathbb{Z}\). The heat equation is given by

\[ \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial ^2 u}{\partial \theta \partial \theta} \]

or equivalently,

\[ u_t = u_{\theta \theta}. \]

To solve this PDE, we require an initial condition:

\[ u(\theta, 0) = u_0 (\theta). \]

We solve this heat equation with the initial value in \(S^1\) by writing

\[ u_0 (\theta) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left ( a_n \sin (n \theta) + b_n \cos (n \theta) \right ) + b_0 \]

which we can always express in this Fourier expansion form provided \(u_0\) is an \(L^2\) function. Then, we can easily check that

\[ u(\theta, t) = \sum_{n\ge 1} e^{-n^2 t} \left ( a_n \sin (n \theta) + b_n \cos (n \theta) \right ) + b_0 \]

is a valid solution for the heat equation. Notice that all the terms except the constant \(b_0\) decay exponentially as time evolves. Intuitively, adopting the heat equation roughly corresponds to the geometric process of smoothing our curve.

docs.title: 1. Curve Shortening Flow is Heat Equation for Curves
docs.text:
Definition 1.1 (Curve shortening flow). Let \(\{\Gamma_t \}_{t \ge 0}\) be a family of simple closed smooth curves embedded in \(\mathbb{R}^2\). We say that \(\Gamma_t\) evolves by a curve shortening flow if every point on \(\Gamma_t\), say \(X\), moves by its curvature vector at \(X \in \Gamma_t\), i.e.,

\[ \partial_t X = \vec{K}. \]

Many differential geometry books follow different conventions for parameterization.

Remark. We provide a counterclockwise parameterization for a simple closed smooth curve during this lecture. Also, we would denote the normal vector \(\vec{N}\) to always refer to the inner part of the simple closed curve. The inner part is defined by the Jordan curve theorem.

docs.title: 1.1 Short Review on Curves
docs.text:
Before we discuss curve shortening flows, we would briefly review curves. Let \(\gamma\) be a parameterization of a curve as

\[ \gamma : S^1 \times [0,T) \to \mathbb{R}^2 , \quad (u,t) \mapsto \gamma(u,t). \]

Definition 1.2 (Curvature vector). Let \(\gamma : I \to \mathbb{R}^2\) be a curve parameterized by arc length \(s\). Then, \(\gamma''(s) = \vec{K}(s)\) is called the curvature vector of \(\gamma\) at \(s\). The size \(\left \vert \vec{K}(s) \right \vert\) is called the curvature and denoted as \(\kappa\).

We denoted the magnitude of curvature vector as \(\kappa\). We would also like to give a notion of direction of curvature vector.

Definition 1.3 (Normal vector). The unit vector \(\vec{N} (s)\) such that \(\gamma''(s) = \kappa \vec{N}(s)\) is called the normal vector of \(\gamma\) at \(s\).

By differentiating \(\gamma'(s) \cdot \gamma'(s) = 1\), we get that \(\gamma''(s) \cdot \gamma'(s) = 0\), which means that \(\vec{N}(s)\) is normal to \(\gamma'(s)\). We also define the unit tangent vector as follows.

Definition 1.4 (Tangent vector). The unit vector \(\vec{T}(s)\) such that \(\vec{T}(s) = \gamma'(s)\) is called the tangent vector of \(\gamma\) at \(s\).

What if we use different parameterization than \(s\)?

Remark. Using \(u\) instead of the reparameterized parameter \(s\), we get

\[ \vec{T} = \frac{\gamma_u}{|\gamma_u|}. \]

Also, we define

\[ g = |\gamma_u| = \frac{ds}{du}. \]

So, the curvature vector is given by

\[ \vec{K} = \frac{\partial \vec{T}}{\partial s} = \frac{1}{g} \frac{\partial \vec{T}}{\partial u} = \frac{1}{g} \left ( \frac{\gamma_u}{g} \right )_u = \frac{g \gamma_{uu} - g_u \gamma_u}{g^3}. \]

If \(\gamma\) is a regular curve, then \(g \ne 0\), which makes the above equation well-defined. Then, we can consider the following:

\[ \vec{K} = \kappa \vec{N} = \vec{T} \wedge \vec{K} = \frac{\gamma_u}{|\gamma_u|} \wedge \vec{K} = \frac{\gamma_u \wedge \gamma_{uu}}{g^3}. \]

So, we can also say that \(\vec{K} = \kappa \vec{N}\) where

\[ \kappa = \frac{\det (\gamma_u , \gamma_{uu})}{g^3}. \]

Now we give an example of a graph function.

Example 1.5. Consider that we have a graph function \(y = f(u)\), i.e., \(\gamma(u) = \left ( u , f(u) \right )\). Then we get the curvature \(\kappa\) as

\[ \kappa = \frac{\begin{vmatrix} 1 & f_u \\ 0 & f_{uu} \end{vmatrix}}{\left ( \left ( 1 + f_u ^2 \right )^{1/2} \right )^3} = \frac{f_{uu}}{\left ( 1 + f_u ^2 \right )^{3/2}}. \]

docs.title: 1.2 Review on Definition of CSF
docs.text:
By reviewing the definition of curve shortening flow using the language of Section 1.1, \(\Gamma_t\) evolves by curve shortening flow if and only if

\[ \gamma_t = \vec{K} = \frac{\det(\gamma_u , \gamma_{uu})}{|\gamma_u|^3} \vec{N}. \]

Example 1.6 (Examples of Curve Shortening Flow).

  1. Consider \(\Gamma_t = \partial B_{r(t)} (0)\) where \(B_r (p)\) is a ball of radius \(r\) centered at \(p\). We have \(\kappa = 1/r(t) > 0\). Then, \(\Gamma_t\) evolves by curve shortening flow if and only if

    \[ \dot{r}(t) = - \frac{1}{r(t)} \implies \frac{1}{2} \left \{ \left ( r(t) \right )^2 \right \}^\prime = -1 \implies r(t) = \sqrt{r_0^2 - 2t}. \]

  2. Consider a graph \(f(u,t)\).

    Exercise. \(\Gamma_t\) evolves by curve shortening flow if and only if \(f\) satisfies the following:

    \[ f_t = \frac{f_{uu}}{\left ( 1 + f_u^2 \right )} \]

    Note the absence of power \(3/2\) compared with the curvature formula for a graph function.

    There is a very well-known solution for this PDE, which is given by the following explicit formula:

    \[ f(u,t) = t - \log (\cos u ) , \quad u \in \left ( - \frac{\pi}{2} , \frac{\pi}{2} \right ). \]

    This is called the Grim reaper solution.

Now we state the main theorem of this course. We first get an intuition from the figure below.

\begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
    \begin{tikzpicture}[
        scale=1,
        >={Stealth[length=2.5mm, width=1.5mm]},
        line join=round,
        line cap=round
    ]
        % Grid and axes (optional, kept subtle)
        \draw[very thin, gray!20, step=1] (-5,-4) grid (5,4);
        \draw[->, gray!50] (-5,0) -- (5,0) node[right] {$x$};
        \draw[->, gray!50] (0,-4) -- (0,4) node[above] {$y$};

        % t = 0 (Initial non-convex "starfish" curve)
        % r(theta) = 3 + 1.2*cos(3*theta)
        \draw [thick, draw=black!85] plot [domain=0:360, samples=200, smooth] 
            ({(3 + 1.2*cos(3*\x))*cos(\x)}, {(3 + 1.2*cos(3*\x))*sin(\x)});
        \node[black!85] at (4.6, 0.4) {$\Gamma_0$};

        % t = t_1 (Convex, slightly elongated curve)
        % r(theta) = 2.2 + 0.3*cos(3*theta)
        \draw [thick, draw=blue!80] plot [domain=0:360, samples=200, smooth] 
            ({(2.2 + 0.3*cos(3*\x))*cos(\x)}, {(2.2 + 0.3*cos(3*\x))*sin(\x)});
        \node[blue!80] at (2.8, 0.8) {$\Gamma_{t_1}$};

        % t = t_2 (More circular, smaller)
        \draw [thick, draw=teal!90] plot [domain=0:360, samples=100, smooth] 
            ({1.2*cos(\x)}, {1.2*sin(\x)});
        \node[teal!90] at (1.4, 0.6) {$\Gamma_{t_2}$};

        % t = t_3 (Shrinking to a round point)
        \draw [thick, draw=magenta!90] plot [domain=0:360, samples=50, smooth] 
            ({0.3*cos(\x)}, {0.3*sin(\x)});
        \node[magenta!90] at (0.5, 0.3) {$\Gamma_{t_3}$};

        % Flow Vectors at t=0 (\partial_t X = \vec{K})
        % Highly convex points (flow inward rapidly)
        % theta = 0
        \draw[->, thick, red] (4.2,0) -- (2.8,0) node[midway, below] {$\vec{K}$};
        % theta = 120
        \draw[->, thick, red] (-2.1, 3.637) -- (-1.4, 2.425) node[midway, right] {$\vec{K}$};
        % theta = 240
        \draw[->, thick, red] (-2.1, -3.637) -- (-1.4, -2.425) node[midway, right] {$\vec{K}$};

        % Non-convex "dents" (flow outward to become convex)
        % theta = 60
        \draw[->, thick, orange] (0.9, 1.558) -- (1.3, 2.25) node[midway, right] {$\vec{K}$};
        % theta = 180
        \draw[->, thick, orange] (-1.8, 0) -- (-2.6, 0) node[midway, below] {$\vec{K}$};
        % theta = 300
        \draw[->, thick, orange] (0.9, -1.558) -- (1.3, -2.25) node[midway, right] {$\vec{K}$};

        % Center point (singularity)
        \filldraw[black] (0,0) circle (1pt);

    \end{tikzpicture}
    \caption{A geometric visualization of curve shortening flow acting on a non-convex curve. The flow velocity is governed by the local curvature vector $\vec{K}$. Regions of high positive curvature (spikes) retract inward (red vectors), whereas regions of negative curvature (dents) are pushed outward (orange vectors). This mechanism guarantees that any simple closed curve will eventually resolve its self-intersections and become perfectly convex, ultimately shrinking to a circular singularity.}
    \label{fig:Intuition of Gage-Hamilton-Grayson thm}
\end{figure}

Theorem 1.7 (Gage-Hamilton-Grayson)12. For any given smooth simple closed curve \(\Gamma_0\) in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), there uniquely exists a solution to the curve shortening flow \(\Gamma_t\) on a maximal finite time interval \([0, T)\). As \(t \to T\), the curve \(\Gamma_t\) becomes asymptotically circular and converges to a single point \(x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^2\). Moreover,

\[ \frac{1}{\sqrt{T-t}} \left ( \Gamma_t - x_0 \right ) \overset{t \nearrow T}{\longrightarrow } \partial B_{\sqrt2} (0) \]

converges smoothly.

Actually, the proof of this remarkable result is historically and mathematically divided into two distinct phases:

  • Gage-Hamilton (1986): This governs the final asymptotic phase. Gage and Hamilton1 proved that once a simple closed curve is strictly convex, it will shrink to a point in finite time, becoming asymptotically circular as it collapses.
  • Grayson (1987): This governs the initial phase of the flow. Grayson2 proved that an arbitrary, non-convex smooth simple closed curve will eventually become strictly convex without ever forming singularities or self-intersections.

However, we would not follow Gage-Hamilton-Grayson's proof of this theorem, but rather we would follow a more modern method throughout this course. We have some reference, a lecture note by R. Haslholfer, Lectures on Curve Shortening Flow3.

docs.title: 1.3 Change of Length and Area
docs.text:
Recall the definition that \(g = |\gamma_u|\), or \(ds = g du\). Then,

\[ \frac{\partial}{\partial t} ds = g_t du , \quad g^2 = \langle \gamma_u , \gamma_u \rangle \implies \left ( g^2 \right )_t = 2gg_t = 2 \langle \gamma_{ut} , \gamma_u \rangle = 2 \langle \gamma_{tu} , \gamma_u \rangle. \]

We know that \(\gamma_u = g \gamma_s = g \vec{T}\) and \(\gamma_t = \kappa \vec{N}\). Because the tangent and normal vectors are orthogonal, \(\langle \gamma_t, \gamma_u \rangle = \langle \kappa \vec{N}, g \vec{T} \rangle = 0\). Taking the spatial derivative \(\partial_u\) of this inner product yields \(\langle \gamma_{tu}, \gamma_u \rangle + \langle \gamma_t, \gamma_{uu} \rangle = 0\). Thus,

\[ \left ( g^2 \right )_t = - 2 \langle \gamma_t , \gamma_{uu} \rangle. \]

Since \(\gamma_u = g \vec{T}\), \(\gamma_{uu} = g_u \vec{T} + g \vec{T}_u = g_u \vec{T} + g \cdot g \vec{T}_s = g_u \vec{T} + g^2 \kappa \vec{N}\). The first term gives \(0\) by taking the inner product with \(\gamma_t = \kappa \vec{N}\), so

\[ \begin{aligned} (g^2 )_t &= 2gg_t = -2g^2 \kappa^2 \\ g_t &= -g \kappa^2 \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial t} ds &= - g\kappa^2 du = - \kappa^2 ds. \end{aligned} \]

Then, we get the evolution of the length of the curve:

\[ L(t) = \int_{S^1} ds , \quad \frac{d}{dt} L(t) = \int_{S^1} - \kappa^2 ds \le 0. \]

Remark. We used \(\gamma_t = \kappa \vec{N}\). But suppose that \(\gamma_t = v \vec{N}\). Then, \(\frac{\partial}{\partial t} ds = - \kappa v ds\).

Now denote \(A(t)\) as the area of the region bounded by \(\Gamma_t\).

Exercise 1.8. Prove that

\[ \frac{d}{dt} A(t) = - \int_{S^1} \kappa ds = -2 \pi. \]

This leads that \(A(t) = A(0) - 2\pi t\).

Corollary 1.9. This is a corollary of Gage-Hamilton-Grayson theorem. We get that the maximal \(T\) is

\[ T = \frac{A(0)}{2\pi} < \infty. \]

Suppose that we are given a simple closed curve \(\Gamma_0\). Our solution cannot exist after this time \(T = \frac{A(0)}{2\pi}\).

Now we give another important theorem, which is the avoidance principle.

Theorem 1.10 (Avoidance principle). Suppose that we are given two curve shortening flows \(\Gamma_t\) and \(\overline{\Gamma}(t)\). Assume that one of them is simple and closed. If \(\Gamma_0\) and \(\overline{\Gamma}(0)\) are disjoint, then \(\Gamma_t\) and \(\overline{\Gamma}(t)\) are disjoint for \(t \ge 0\) as long as solutions exist.

Moreover, we can define the distance

\[ d(t) = \operatorname{dist} (\Gamma_t , \overline{\Gamma}(t)) = \inf \left \{d(p,q) \mid p \in \Gamma_t , \; q \in \overline{\Gamma}(t) \right \}. \]

Then, \(d(t)\) is non-decreasing in \(t\).

Proof. Since at least one of the curves is simple and closed (which implies it is compact), the infimum of the distance between them is strictly achieved. Thus, for any time \(t\), there exist points \(p \in \Gamma_t\) and \(q \in \overline{\Gamma}(t)\) such that \(d(t) = \operatorname{dist}(p, q)\).

Because \(p\) and \(q\) minimize the distance between the two curves, the line segment connecting them must be perpendicular to the tangent spaces of both curves. Therefore, the normal vectors at \(p\) and \(q\) are collinear. Assuming they are oriented in the same direction, we have \(N(p) = \overline{N}(q) = N\).

Furthermore, looking at the local geometry at these closest points, the inner curve \(\overline{\Gamma}(t)\) must be bounded by the outer curve \(\Gamma_t\). By comparing their osculating circles, the inner curve must have a curvature greater than or equal to that of the outer curve to avoid intersection:

\[ \overline{\kappa}(q) \ge \kappa(p). \]

Under the curve shortening flow, the points evolve with normal velocities \(\partial_t p = \kappa(p) N\) and \(\partial_t q = \overline{\kappa}(q) N\). The rate of change of the distance \(d(t)\) is determined entirely by the relative velocity of these points projected onto the unit vector connecting them:

\[ \frac{d}{dt} d(t) = \langle \partial_t q - \partial_t p , N \rangle = \langle \overline{\kappa}(q) N - \kappa(p) N , N \rangle = \overline{\kappa}(q) - \kappa(p). \]

Since we established from the geometric containment that \(\overline{\kappa}(q) \ge \kappa(p)\), it directly follows that:

\[ \frac{d}{dt} d(t) \ge 0. \]

Because the inner curve moves inward faster than the outer curve, \(d(t)\) is a non-decreasing function of \(t\). Consequently, if the curves are initially disjoint (\(d(0) > 0\)), they must remain disjoint (\(d(t) \ge d(0) > 0\)) for as long as the flows exist. \(\blacksquare\)

Now we give a corollary.

Corollary 1.11. Suppose that \(\Gamma_0\) is included in the inner part of \(\partial B_R (0)\). Then, by Corollary 1.9 and Theorem 1.10 (Avoidance principle), \(\Gamma_t\) cannot exist beyond \(R^2 / 2\).

  1. Gage, M., & Hamilton, R. S. (1986). The heat equation shrinking convex plane curves. Journal of Differential Geometry, 23(1), 69-96. ↩↩

  2. Grayson, M. A. (1987). The heat equation shrinks embedded plane curves to round points. Journal of Differential Geometry, 26(2), 285-314. ↩↩

  3. Haslhofer, R. (2026). Lectures on curve shortening flow. arXiv preprint arXiv:2604.01981. ↩

docs.title: Evolution Equations
docs.text:
In the previous section, we derived that \(\partial_t ds = - \kappa^2 ds\). This showed that the length of the curve decreases.

\[ \dot{L}(t) = \int_{\Gamma_t} -\kappa^2 ds \le 0 \]

docs.title: 2.1 Evolution of Geometric Quantities
docs.text:
The strictly decreasing nature of the curve's length provides a powerful geometric intuition: the flow acts like a perfectly elastic rubber band dissipating energy. If we constrain this rubber band by fixing its endpoints, it must continuously contract until it reaches the absolute minimum of the length functional for that boundary condition.

Corollary 2.1. Let \(\Gamma_0\) be a curve segment with two fixed endpoints. If \(\Gamma_t\) evolves by curve shortening flow subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions (the endpoints remain fixed for all \(t\)), the curve asymptotically evolves into a straight line connecting the two points.

While it is geometrically intuitive that the curve shortening flow decreases total length, understanding the exact evolution of the curve's geometry requires us to track how differential operators interact along the flow. Because the arc-length parameter \(s\) depends on the time-evolving metric \(g\), the time derivative \(\partial_t\) and the spatial derivative \(\partial_s\) do not commute. We must first establish their commutator relation to derive the evolution equations for the curve's intrinsic quantities.

Lemma 2.2.

\[ \left [ \partial_t , \partial_s \right ] = \kappa^2 \partial_s \]

That is,

\[ \partial_t \partial_s f - \partial_s \partial_t f = \kappa^2 \partial_s f. \]

Proof. We know that

\[ \begin{aligned} \partial_s f = \frac{1}{g} \frac{\partial f}{\partial u} \implies \partial_t \partial_s f &= \frac{1}{g} \frac{\partial ^2 f}{\partial t \partial u} - \frac{g_t}{g^2} \frac{\partial f}{\partial u} \\ &= \frac{1}{g} \frac{\partial ^2 f}{\partial u \partial t} + \kappa^2 \frac{\partial f}{\partial s} \end{aligned} \]

\(\blacksquare\)

For example, we compute \(\left ( T_s \right )_t\).

Example 2.3. For example,

\[ \begin{aligned} T_t = \gamma_{st} &= \gamma_{ts} + \kappa ^2 \gamma_s \\ &= \left ( \kappa N \right )_s + \kappa ^2 T \\ &= \kappa_s N. \end{aligned} \]

Similarly,

\[ N_t = - \kappa_s T \]

holds. Also, we get \(\kappa_t\) from the following.

\[ \begin{aligned} \left ( T_s \right )_t &= T_{ts} + \kappa^2 T_s \\ &= \left ( \kappa_s N \right )_s + \kappa^3 N \\ &= \kappa_{ss} N - \kappa_s \kappa T + \kappa^3 N \end{aligned} \]

But, \((T_s)_t\) also satisfies

\[ (T_s)_t = (\kappa N)_t = \kappa_t N + \kappa N_t. \]

Then, by equating the normal terms, we get

\[ \kappa_t = \kappa_{ss} + \kappa^3. \]

docs.title: 2.2 The Maximum Principle and Convexity
docs.text:
The evolution equation \(\kappa_t = \kappa_{ss} + \kappa^3\) is a standard reaction-diffusion equation, revealing the competing forces within the flow. The diffusion term (\(\kappa_{ss}\)) acts to smooth out variations in curvature, while the nonlinear reaction term (\(\kappa^3\)) drives the curvature toward finite-time blow-up at highly curved regions. To rigorously analyze which force dominates and how the curvature is bounded, we rely on the fundamental tool for parabolic PDEs: the maximum principle.

Theorem 2.4 (Maximum principle). Suppose that \(\left ( \partial_t - \partial_{ss} \right ) u \le 0\) for \(u \in \mathcal{C}^{2,1} (S^1 \times [0,T])\). Then,

\[ \max_{S^1} u(\cdot , t) \le \max_{S^1} u( \cdot , 0) \]

for all \(t \ge 0\).

Proof. Let \(M = \max_{x \in S^1} u(x, 0)\). We want to show that \(u(x,t) \le M\) for all \((x,t) \in S^1 \times [0,T]\).

We proceed by contradiction. To avoid edge cases where spatial derivatives might vanish without yielding a strict sign, we introduce a small perturbation. For any \(\varepsilon > 0\), define a new function

\[ u_\varepsilon (x,t) = u(x,t) - \varepsilon t. \]

Applying the heat operator to \(u_\varepsilon\), we find

\[ \left ( \partial_t - \partial_{ss} \right ) u_\varepsilon = \left ( \partial_t - \partial_{ss} \right ) u - \varepsilon. \]

Since we are given that \((\partial_t - \partial_{ss}) u \le 0\), it follows strictly that

\[ \left ( \partial_t - \partial_{ss} \right ) u_\varepsilon \le -\varepsilon < 0. \]

Now, assume for the sake of contradiction that the theorem is false. This means there is some point where \(u(x,t) > M\). If so, for a sufficiently small \(\varepsilon > 0\), there must also exist some point where \(u_\varepsilon(x,t) > M\).

Since \(S^1 \times [0,T]\) is compact and \(u_\varepsilon(x,0) = u(x,0) \le M\), there must exist a first time \(t_0 > 0\) and a spatial point \(x_0 \in S^1\) such that

\[ u_\varepsilon(x_0, t_0) = M \quad \text{and} \quad u_\varepsilon(x, t) \le M \text{ for all } x \in S^1, \, t \le t_0. \]

At this point \((x_0, t_0)\), the function \(u_\varepsilon\) attains a local spatial maximum, which implies two necessary conditions from elementary calculus

\[ \partial_s u_\varepsilon(x_0, t_0) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \partial_{ss} u_\varepsilon(x_0, t_0) \le 0. \]

Furthermore, because \(t_0\) is the very first time the function reaches the value \(M\) (it was strictly less than or equal to \(M\) for all \(t < t_0\)), the function must be non-decreasing in time at that instant

\[ \partial_t u_\varepsilon(x_0, t_0) \ge 0. \]

Combining these calculus facts, we evaluate the heat operator at \((x_0, t_0)\)

\[ \left ( \partial_t - \partial_{ss} \right ) u_\varepsilon(x_0, t_0) \ge 0 - 0 = 0. \]

However, this directly contradicts our earlier strict derivation that \((\partial_t - \partial_{ss}) u_\varepsilon < 0\) everywhere on the domain.

Because of this contradiction, our assumption must be false. Therefore, \(u_\varepsilon(x,t) \le M\) for all \((x,t)\). Taking the limit as \(\varepsilon \to 0\) yields

\[ u(x,t) \le M = \max_{x \in S^1} u(x, 0), \]

which completes the proof. \(\blacksquare\)

Now we give a corollary about time evolution of bound of curvature.

Corollary 2.5. Suppose that the curvature is bounded by

\[ \kappa(\cdot , 0) \ge m_0 > 0. \]

Then, for \(t > 0\), \(\kappa(\cdot , t) \ge m_0\). Moreover,

\[ \kappa(\cdot , t) \ge \frac{m_0}{\sqrt{1-2m_0 ^2 t}} \]

where the (RHS) is the solution to the ODE \(\dot{f} = f^3\) with \(f(0) = m_0\).

Proof.

Step 0 : Skeleton of Proof We prove by using the maximum principle. We would first prove the following statement, which implies our corollary.

Step 1 : General Statement Suppose that there are two functions \(f_1 ( u,t)\) and \(f_2 (u,t)\) satisfying

\[ (f_1)_t - (f_1)_{ss} = f_1 ^3 , \quad (f_2)_t - (f_2)_{ss} < f_2 ^3 \]

and \(f_1 > f_2\) at \(t=0\). Then, \(f_1 \ge f_2\) for \(t \ge 0\), \(u \in S^1\).

Step 2 : Proof of General Statement We prove the statement above. Suppose not, that is, there exist a first time \((t_0 , u_0)\) such that \(f_1 = f_2\). At this point,

\[ f_1 = f_2, \quad (f_1 - f_2)_t\le 0, \quad (f_1 - f_2)_{ss} \ge 0. \]

Then,

\[ 0 = (f_1)_t - (f_1)_{ss} - f_1 ^3 \le (f_2)_t - (f_2)_{ss} - f_2 ^3 < 0 \]

which gives a contradiction.

Step 3 : Implication to Corollary Let \(f_1(s,t) = \kappa(s,t)\). From our earlier derivation, the evolution equation for curvature under curve shortening flow is \(\kappa_t = \kappa_{ss} + \kappa^3\). Therefore, \(f_1\) exactly satisfies the parabolic equation \((f_1)_t - (f_1)_{ss} = f_1^3\).

To apply the strict inequality from Step 1, we introduce a small constant \(\varepsilon > 0\) and define \(f_2^\varepsilon(t)\) as the spatially independent solution to the perturbed ODE

\[ \frac{d}{dt} f_2^\varepsilon(t) = (f_2^\varepsilon(t))^3 - \varepsilon \]

with the initial condition \(f_2^\varepsilon(0) = m_0 - \varepsilon\).

Since \(f_2^\varepsilon\) is independent of the spatial parameter \(s\), we have \((f_2^\varepsilon)_{ss} = 0\). Thus, it satisfies the strict subsolution condition

\[ (f_2^\varepsilon)_t - (f_2^\varepsilon)_{ss} = (f_2^\varepsilon)^3 - \varepsilon < (f_2^\varepsilon)^3. \]

At the initial time \(t=0\), we are given \(\kappa(\cdot, 0) \ge m_0\). Therefore, we have a strict ordering of the initial data

\[ f_1(\cdot, 0) = \kappa(\cdot, 0) \ge m_0 > m_0 - \varepsilon = f_2^\varepsilon(0). \]

Since all the hypotheses of Step 1 are satisfied, we conclude that \(f_1(\cdot, t) \ge f_2^\varepsilon(t)\) for all valid \(t \ge 0\).

Now, by taking the limit as \(\varepsilon \to 0\), the function \(f_2^\varepsilon(t)\) converges smoothly to \(f(t)\), where \(f(t)\) is the exact solution to \(\dot{f} = f^3\) with \(f(0) = m_0\). Solving this separable ODE yields

\[ f(t) = \frac{m_0}{\sqrt{1 - 2m_0^2 t}}. \]

Thus, the limit gives us our primary bound

\[ \kappa(\cdot, t) \ge \frac{m_0}{\sqrt{1 - 2m_0^2 t}}. \]

Finally, since \(t \ge 0\), we know that \(\sqrt{1 - 2m_0^2 t} \le 1\). This implies that \(f(t) \ge m_0\), which immediately guarantees \(\kappa(\cdot, t) \ge m_0\). This completes the proof. \(\blacksquare\)

The previous bound strictly applies to curves with strictly positive initial curvature. However, by taking the limit as the initial minimum curvature \(m_0 \searrow 0\), we immediately obtain one of the most fundamental shape-preserving properties of the curve shortening flow: convexity is preserved.

Corollary 2.6. If a curve is convex, i.e., \(\kappa \ge 0\) for \(t=0\), then the curve is convex for \(t > 0\), that is, \(\kappa \ge 0\) for \(t > 0\).

docs.title: 2.3 Short-Time Existence
docs.text:
We have established that convex curves remain convex and that curvature cannot jump from positive to negative. However, this does not guarantee the flow exists indefinitely. The nonlinear nature of the curvature evolution strongly suggests that the geometry will eventually collapse. To formalize this, we must first establish that a unique solution exists, at least for a short time, and then identify the precise mechanism that forces the flow to terminate.

Theorem 2.7 (Short time existence). Let \(\Gamma_0\) be a \(\mathcal{C}^\infty\) simple closed curve. Then, the curve shortening flow \(\Gamma_t\) exists for a short time \(t \in [0,T)\) for \(T < \infty\). Here, \(\Gamma_t\) is smooth, simple, closed, and the solution is unique. Moreover, if \(T\) is the maximal time of existence, then

\[ \max_{\Gamma_t} \kappa \nearrow \infty \quad \text{as} \quad t \nearrow T. \]

How far can we expand the curve shortening flow?

Theorem 2.8. Suppose that \(\Gamma_t\) is a curve shortening flow for \(t\in [0,T)\) and \(\sup_{\Gamma_t} |\kappa| < C < \infty\) for \(0 \le t \le T\). Then, \(\Gamma_t\) can be extended to \(t\in [0,T+\varepsilon)\).

The extension theorem dictates that the flow can only terminate if the curvature itself blows up. However, merely bounding the scalar curvature is not obviously sufficient to guarantee that the curve's higher-order geometry doesn't develop microscopic kinks. To seamlessly extend the flow, we must ensure that all geometric derivatives remain perfectly controlled. Because curve shortening flow is a parabolic system, it instantly smooths out rough initial data, yielding the following Bernstein-Bando-Shi type estimates.

Theorem 2.9. Suppose that \(|\kappa| \le A <\infty\) for \(t \in [0,T]\). Then,

\[ \left \vert \partial_s ^m \kappa \right \vert \le C \cdot \frac{1}{t^{m/2}} \]

for some \(C = C(A,T) < \infty\).

Proof.

Step 1 : \(m=1\) We have

\[ \begin{aligned} \kappa_t &= \kappa_{ss} + \kappa^3 \\ \kappa_{ts} &= \kappa_{sss} + 3 \kappa^2 \kappa_s \\ \kappa_{st} &= \kappa_{sss} + 3 \kappa^2 \kappa_s + \kappa^2 \kappa_s \\ &= \kappa_{sss} + 4 \kappa^2 \kappa_s. \end{aligned} \]

So, we have that \(\partial_t \kappa_s - \partial_{ss} \kappa_s = 4 \kappa^2 \kappa_s\). Now we calculate the following for a reason that is used after.

\[ \begin{aligned} \partial_t (\kappa_s )^2 - \partial_{ss} (\kappa_s )^2 &= 2 \kappa_s (4\kappa^2 \kappa_s) - 2 \kappa_{ss}^2 \\ &= 8 \kappa^2 \kappa_s ^2 - 2 \kappa_{ss}^2 \end{aligned} \]

Also,

\[ \partial_t \kappa^2 - \partial_{ss} \kappa^2 = 2 \kappa^4 - 2 \kappa_s ^2. \]

Consider some function \(f = t \kappa_s ^2 + \beta \kappa^2\) for \(0 < \beta < \infty\). By the computation above,

\[ f_t - f_{ss} = 8t \kappa^2 \kappa_s ^2 - t \kappa_{ss}^2 + \kappa_s ^2 + \beta \left (2\kappa^4 - 2 \kappa_s ^2 \right ) \]

By choosing \(\beta\) large enough, this is bounded by some constant \(2 \beta A^4\). Also, suppose that \(f(0) \le \beta A^2\). By the maximal principle, \(f \le g\) where \(g\) solves

\[ \dot{g} = 2 \beta A^4 , \quad g(0) = \beta A^2, \]

which gives \(f \le C\). Then, this also implies that \(t \kappa_s ^2 \le C\), and thus

\[ |\kappa_s| \le \frac{1}{\sqrt{t}} C. \]

Step 2 : \(m > 1\) For \(m>1\), we can set an appropriate \(f\), and bound it by \(C \cdot 1/t^{m/2}\). \(\blacksquare\)

Precise proof for part 2 requires advanced knowledge in PDE.

Remark. We can now explicitly see how Theorem 2.9 implies the extension in Theorem 2.8. If the magnitude of the curvature \(|\kappa|\) remains uniformly bounded as \(t \to T\), the derivative estimates guarantee that all higher-order spatial derivatives of the curvature are also uniformly bounded. This translates to uniform bounds on all derivatives of the position vector \(\gamma\). By providing both uniform boundedness and equicontinuity, these bounds satisfy the exact conditions needed for the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem. Thus, we can extract a smoothly converging limit, proving that \(\Gamma_t \to \Gamma_T\) as a perfectly well-defined \(\mathcal{C}^\infty\) curve. Because \(\Gamma_T\) is smooth, we can simply apply the short-time existence theorem using \(\Gamma_T\) as our new initial data, thereby extending the flow seamlessly into \([0, T+\varepsilon)\).

Because all higher-order derivatives are controlled solely by the maximum of the curvature, the geometry cannot degenerate in wild, unpredictable ways. This strict control over the curve's regularity forces a stark conclusion: the flow must eventually encounter a definitive singularity where the maximum curvature strictly diverges to infinity.

Corollary 2.10. Let \(\Gamma_0\) be a \(\mathcal{C}^\infty\) simple closed curve. Then, there exists a unique \(T< \infty\) such that

\[ \sup_{t<T} \sup_{\Gamma_t} \kappa = \infty. \]

Here, \(T\) is called the singular time.

docs.title: 2.4 Rescaling and Singularity Formation
docs.text:
By Theorem 2.8 and the definition of the singular time \(T\), we know that the flow develops a singularity precisely because the curvature blows up to infinity. To understand the geometric shape of the curve as it collapses, we must "zoom in" on the singularity both in space and in time. Because the curve shortening flow is governed by a heat-type equation, the natural way to blow up the singularity is via parabolic rescaling, which preserves the structure of the flow equation.

Lemma 2.11. Let \(\Gamma_t\) be a curve shortening flow. Then, for \(\Lambda > 0\), \( ilde{\Gamma}_t = \Lambda \Gamma_{t/\Lambda^2}\) is also a curve shortening flow.

Proof. Let \( ilde{\gamma}(u,t) = \Lambda \gamma(u, t/\Lambda^2)\). Taking the time derivative yields

\[ \partial_t ilde{\gamma} = \Lambda \cdot rac{1}{\Lambda^2} \partial_ au \gamma = rac{1}{\Lambda} \vec{K} \]

where \( au = t/\Lambda^2\). For the scaled curve, the normal vector is unchanged (\( ilde{N} = N\)), but the spatial derivatives scale inversely, meaning the new curvature is \( ilde{\kappa} = rac{1}{\Lambda} \kappa\). Therefore, the new curvature vector is \(\vec{ ilde{K}} = ilde{\kappa} ilde{N} = rac{1}{\Lambda} \vec{K}\).

Substituting this back, we get \(\partial_t ilde{\gamma} = \vec{ ilde{K}}\), which perfectly satisfies the curve shortening flow equation. \( lacksquare\)

Now we look for some monotone quantities along the curve shortening flow. We know that

\[ \dot{L} = - \int_{\Gamma_t} \kappa^2 ds \le 0 \]

is monotone. However, this is not a good quantity since it varies by rescaling.

There exists some good monotone quantity, namely weighted length. When studying how curves shrink near singularities, the weighted length is usually used.

For given \(X_0 = (x_0 , t_0)\) as the spacetime point of the singularity, the weight, specifically backward heat kernel is given by

\[ ho_{X_0}(x,t) = rac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi (t_0 - t)}} e^{- rac{|x-x_0|^2}{4(t_0 - t)}} \]

for \(t < t_0\), \(x \in \mathbb{R}^2\). We define the weighted length as

\[ \Phi_{X_0} (t) = \int_{\Gamma_t} ho_{X_0} (x , t) ds(x). \]

We can check that \(\Phi_{X_0}\) is rescaling invariant.

Remark. To verify that the weighted length \(\Phi_{X_0}(t)\) is invariant under parabolic rescaling, we perform a change of variables centered at the singularity \(X_0 = (x_0, t_0)\).

Define the rescaled space and time coordinates as

\[ ilde{x} = \Lambda(x-x_0), \quad au = \Lambda^2 (t-t_0) \]

where \(\Lambda > 0\). Under this transformation, the singular point \(X_0\) is mapped to the origin in the new coordinates, so our new base point is \( ilde{X}_0 = (0,0)\).

First, we calculate how the backward heat kernel \( ho\) transforms. In the rescaled coordinates, the weight function evaluated around the new origin is

\[ ho_{(0,0)}( ilde{x}, au) = rac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi (- au)}} \exp\left({- rac{| ilde{x}|^2}{4(- au)}} ight). \]

Substituting our definitions for \( ilde{x}\) and \( au\) into this expression yields

\[ egin{aligned} ho_{(0,0)}( ilde{x}, au) &= rac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi (-\Lambda^2(t-t_0))}} \exp\left({- rac{|\Lambda(x-x_0)|^2}{4(-\Lambda^2(t-t_0))}} ight) \ &= rac{1}{\Lambda \sqrt{4\pi (t_0-t)}} \exp\left({- rac{\Lambda^2|x-x_0|^2}{4\Lambda^2(t_0-t)}} ight) \ &= rac{1}{\Lambda} ho_{X_0}(x, t). \end{aligned} \]

Next, we consider the arc length measure. Because the rescaled curve \( ilde{\Gamma}_ au\) is a pure spatial dilation of \(\Gamma_t\) (shifted by \(x_0\)) by a factor of \(\Lambda\), the 1-dimensional arc length element scales linearly

\[ d ilde{s}( ilde{x}) = \Lambda \, ds(x). \]

Finally, we evaluate the total weighted length of the rescaled curve

\[ egin{aligned} \Phi_{(0,0)}( au) &= \int_{ ilde{\Gamma}_ au} ho_{(0,0)}( ilde{x}, au) d ilde{s}( ilde{x}) \ &= \int_{\Gamma_t} \left( rac{1}{\Lambda} ho_{X_0}(x, t) ight) ig( \Lambda \, ds(x) ig) \ &= \int_{\Gamma_t} ho_{X_0}(x, t) ds(x) \ &= \Phi_{X_0}(t). \end{aligned} \]

This precise cancelation of the scaling factor \(\Lambda\) demonstrates that the weighted length functional is perfectly invariant under parabolic rescaling.

Now we introduce a theorem that shows the monotonicity of the weighted length \(\Phi_{X_0}\).

Theorem 2.12 (Huisken)1.

\[ rac{d}{dt} \Phi_{X_0} (t) = - \int_{\Gamma_t} \left( \kappa + rac{\langle x - x_0 , N angle}{2 (t_0 - t)} ight)^2 ho_{X_0} ds \le 0. \]

Proof. The time derivative of the weighted length functional is given by

\[ rac{d}{dt} \Phi_{X_0}(t) = rac{d}{dt} \int_{\Gamma_t} ho_{X_0} ds = \int_{\Gamma_t} \left( rac{d}{dt} ho_{X_0} ight) ds + \int_{\Gamma_t} ho_{X_0} (\partial_t ds). \]

From our earlier evolution equations, we know that the arc length measure evolves as \(\partial_t ds = -\kappa^2 ds\). By the chain rule, the total time derivative of the weight \( ho_{X_0}(x(t), t)\) along the flow \(\partial_t x = \kappa N\) is

\[ rac{d}{dt} ho_{X_0} = \partial_t ho_{X_0} + \langle abla ho_{X_0} , \partial_t x angle = \partial_t ho_{X_0} + \kappa \langle abla ho_{X_0} , N angle. \]

Direct differentiation of the backward heat kernel \( ho_{X_0}(x,t) = (4\pi(t_0-t))^{-1/2} \exp\left(- rac{|x-x_0|^2}{4(t_0-t)} ight)\) yields

\[ \partial_t ho_{X_0} = ho_{X_0} \left[ rac{1}{2(t_0 - t)} - rac{|x-x_0|^2}{4(t_0 - t)^2} ight], \quad abla ho_{X_0} = - ho_{X_0} rac{x-x_0}{2(t_0 - t)}. \]

Substituting these into our integral, we get the raw evolution equation

\[ rac{d}{dt} \Phi_{X_0}(t) = \int_{\Gamma_t} ho_{X_0} \left[ rac{1}{2(t_0 - t)} - rac{|x-x_0|^2}{4(t_0 - t)^2} - \kappa rac{\langle x-x_0, N angle}{2(t_0 - t)} - \kappa^2 ight] ds. ag{2.1} \]

To complete the square, we use integration by parts on the spatial derivative along the curve. The tangential derivative of \( ho_{X_0}\) is

\[ \partial_s ho_{X_0} = \langle abla ho_{X_0}, T angle = - ho_{X_0} rac{\langle x-x_0, T angle}{2(t_0 - t)}. \]

Because \(\Gamma_t\) is a closed curve, the integral of any exact spatial derivative vanishes. We consider the integral of \(\partial_s \left( ho_{X_0} rac{\langle x-x_0, T angle}{2(t_0-t)} ight)\)

\[ 0 = \int_{\Gamma_t} \partial_s \left( ho_{X_0} rac{\langle x-x_0, T angle}{2(t_0 - t)} ight) ds. \]

Applying the product rule and using \(\partial_s (x-x_0) = T\) and the Frenet-Serret formula \(\partial_s T = \kappa N\), we get

\[ 0 = \int_{\Gamma_t} \left[ \partial_s ho_{X_0} rac{\langle x-x_0, T angle}{2(t_0 - t)} + ho_{X_0} rac{\langle T, T angle + \langle x-x_0, \kappa N angle}{2(t_0 - t)} ight] ds. \]

Substituting our identity for \(\partial_s ho_{X_0}\) and using \(\langle T, T angle = 1\), this becomes

\[ 0 = \int_{\Gamma_t} ho_{X_0} \left[ - rac{\langle x-x_0, T angle^2}{4(t_0 - t)^2} + rac{1}{2(t_0 - t)} + rac{\kappa \langle x-x_0, N angle}{2(t_0 - t)} ight] ds. \]

We now use the geometric decomposition \(|x-x_0|^2 = \langle x-x_0, T angle^2 + \langle x-x_0, N angle^2\) and subtract this zero-valued integral from our raw evolution equation (2.1).

The \( rac{1}{2(t_0-t)}\) terms cancel completely. Furthermore, the tangential components \( rac{\langle x-x_0, T angle^2}{4(t_0-t)^2}\) cancel out perfectly, leaving only the normal components and the curvature terms

\[ rac{d}{dt} \Phi_{X_0}(t) = \int_{\Gamma_t} ho_{X_0} \left[ - rac{\langle x-x_0, N angle^2}{4(t_0 - t)^2} - rac{2\kappa\langle x-x_0, N angle}{2(t_0 - t)} - \kappa^2 ight] ds. \]

Factoring out the negative sign completes the perfect square

\[ rac{d}{dt} \Phi_{X_0}(t) = - \int_{\Gamma_t} \left( \kappa + rac{\langle x - x_0 , N angle}{2 (t_0 - t)} ight)^2 ho_{X_0} ds. \]

Since the backward heat kernel \( ho_{X_0}\) is strictly positive and the squared term is non-negative, the entire integrand is non-negative. Thus, the time derivative is strictly \(\le 0\), which completes the proof. \( lacksquare\)

Notice that this monotonicity is strict unless the term inside the square vanishes identically.

Remark. The equality case in Huisken's theorem precisely characterizes the self-similar shrinkers of the flow. By the Abresch-Langer classification theorem (1986), the only embedded self-shrinkers in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) are the straight line through the origin and the circle. Thus, any singularity modeled by an embedded shrinker must be asymptotically round.

  1. Huisken, G. (1998). A distance comparison principle for evolving curves. Asian Journal of Mathematics, 2, 127-133. ↩

docs.title: 3.1 Gaussian Density and Local Regularity
docs.text:
Definition 3.1.1 (Gaussian density). The Gaussian density at \(X_0 = (x_0 , t_0)\) with scale \(\gamma > 0\) is defined by

\[ \Theta(\Gamma_t , X_0 , \gamma) = \int_{\Gamma_{t_0 - \gamma^2}}\rho_{X_0} (x , t_0 - \gamma^2 ) dx \; \left ( = \Phi_{X_0} (t_0 - \gamma^2) \right ) \]

With this localized mass measure in hand, we can establish a crucial regularity condition that restricts the maximum curvature whenever the density is sufficiently close to that of a flat line.

Theorem 3.1.2 (Local regularity theorem)1. There exist \(\varepsilon > 0\), \(C< \infty\) such that the following holds. Let \(\Gamma_t\) be the curve shortening flow for \(t \in (t_0 - 4 \gamma^2 , t_0)\). If \(\sup \Theta(\Gamma , Y , \gamma) \le 1+ \varepsilon\), for \(Y \in B_r (x_0) \times (t_0 - \gamma^2 ,t_0) := P_\gamma (x_0 , t_0)\), then

\[ \sup_{P_{\gamma/2}(x_0 , t_0)} \kappa \le \frac{C}{\gamma}. \]

Proof. Assume for the sake of contradiction that the theorem is false. Then, there exists a sequence of curve shortening flows, \(\Gamma_t^i\) for \(t \in (-4, 0 )\), such that:

  • \(\Theta ( \Gamma_t^i , X , 1) < 1 + \frac{1}{i}\) for all \(X \in P_1 (0)\),
  • and there exists \(X_i \in P_{1/2} (0)\) such that \(\kappa (X_i) \ge i\).

Claim: There exists a spacetime point \(Y_i = (y_i, t_i) \in P_{3/4} (0)\) with \(\kappa (Y_i) := \kappa_i \ge i\) such that \(\kappa \le 2 \kappa_i\) on the parabolic neighborhood \(P_{\frac{i}{10 \kappa_i}} (Y_i)\).

(The proof of this claim follows via the point selection argument, deferred below).

Assuming the claim holds, we define our parabolically rescaled flow centered at \(Y_i\) as:

\[ \tilde{\Gamma}_t^i = \kappa_i \left( \Gamma_{t_i + \frac{t}{\kappa_i^2}}^i - y_i \right). \]

Under this parabolic rescaling, the geometry and bounds transform such that:

\[ \tilde{\kappa}^i (0,0) = 1 , \quad \text{and} \quad \tilde{\kappa}^i \le 2 \quad \text{on} \quad P_{\frac{i}{10}} (0). \]

Because the rescaled curvature is uniformly bounded by 2 on expanding domains (since \(i \to \infty\)), all higher-order derivatives are also uniformly bounded. Thus, we can extract a smoothly convergent limit sequence, denoted as \(\tilde{\Gamma}_t^\infty\), which is an eternal solution.

Moreover, by the density assumption of the theorem, taking the limit \(i \to \infty\) forces the Gaussian density of the limit flow to be exactly 1 at all scales:

\[ \Theta(\tilde{\Gamma}_t^\infty , X , r) = 1 \quad \forall X \in \mathbb{R}^2 \times (-\infty, 0], \,\, \forall r > 0. \]

By Huisken's monotonicity formula, the constancy of the density implies that \(\tilde{\Gamma}^\infty\) must be a self-shrinker. The only embedded self-shrinkers are the straight line and the shrinking circle.

However, the Gaussian density of a shrinking circle is strictly greater than 1, contradicting \(\Theta \equiv 1\). Therefore, \(\tilde{\Gamma}^\infty\) must be a straight line. But a straight line has curvature identically zero, which directly contradicts our condition that \(\tilde{\kappa}^\infty(0,0) = 1\). This completes the contradiction. \(\blacksquare\)

Consequently, this forces the realization that any sequence approaching a singularity under these density constraints cannot logically model anything other than a trivial flat line.

Remark. Alternatively, suppose that a rescaled solution \(\Lambda \Gamma_{t / \Lambda^2}\) converges to a straight line. By the multiplicity one conjecture, if \(\Lambda \gg 1\), then \(\Theta (\Lambda \Gamma_{t/ \Lambda^2} , 0 , 1) \approx 1\). Consequently, \(\Lambda \Gamma_{t/\Lambda^2}\) must have \(\kappa \le C\), which yields a similar contradiction if we assume unbounded curvature. Therefore, a straight line cannot manifest as the singularity model in this context.

To rigorously justify the local curvature bounds that allowed us to extract the rescaled limit sequence above, we now detail the deferred point selection argument.

Proof of claim. This is an application of the point selection argument2.

We construct a sequence of points iteratively. Let \(Y_i^0 = X_i\). By our initial assumptions, \(Y_i^0 \in P_{1/2}(0)\) and \(\kappa(Y_i^0) \ge i\).

If \(Y_i^0\) satisfies the claim (i.e., \(\kappa \le 2\kappa(Y_i^0)\) on \(P_{\frac{i}{10\kappa(Y_i^0)}}(Y_i^0)\)), we set \(Y_i = Y_i^0\) and terminate the sequence.

If not, there exists a point \(Y_i^1 \in P_{\frac{i}{10\kappa(Y_i^0)}}(Y_i^0)\) such that \(\kappa(Y_i^1) > 2\kappa(Y_i^0)\).

Iterating this process, if \(Y_i^k\) does not satisfy the claim, we can find \(Y_i^{k+1} \in P_{\frac{i}{10\kappa(Y_i^k)}}(Y_i^k)\) such that \(\kappa(Y_i^{k+1}) > 2\kappa(Y_i^k)\).

Observe that \(\kappa(Y_i^k) > 2^k \kappa(Y_i^0) \ge 2^k i\). Since the curve shortening flow is smooth on the given time interval, the curvature must be finite on compact subsets, meaning this sequence cannot continue indefinitely. It must terminate at some finite step \(m\). The terminal point \(Y_i^m\) satisfies the local curvature bound, so we define our desired point as \(Y_i = Y_i^m\).

It remains to show that this terminal point \(Y_i\) actually remains within \(P_{3/4}(0)\). By the triangle inequality for the parabolic distance, the distance from the initial point \(Y_i^0\) to \(Y_i^k\) is bounded by the sum of the radii of the nested neighborhoods:

\[ |Y_i^k - Y_i^0| \le \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} \frac{i}{10\kappa(Y_i^j)}. \]

Since \(\kappa(Y_i^j) > 2^j \kappa(Y_i^0)\), we can bound the series by a geometric progression:

\[ |Y_i^k - Y_i^0| \le \frac{i}{10\kappa(Y_i^0)} \left( 1 + \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{4} + \cdots \right) = \frac{i}{10\kappa(Y_i^0)} (2) = \frac{i}{5\kappa(Y_i^0)}. \]

Because the initial curvature \(\kappa(Y_i^0) \ge i\), we have \(\frac{i}{\kappa(Y_i^0)} \le 1\). Thus:

\[ |Y_i^k - Y_i^0| \le \frac{1}{5}. \]

Furthermore, since \(Y_i^0 = X_i \in P_{1/2}(0)\), its distance to the origin is \(|Y_i^0 - 0| \le \frac{1}{2}\). Therefore:

\[ |Y_i^k| \le |Y_i^0 - 0| + |Y_i^k - Y_i^0| \le \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{5} = \frac{7}{10} < \frac{3}{4}. \]

This confirms that \(Y_i \in P_{3/4}(0)\), completing the proof of the claim. \(\blacksquare\)

Let \(\Gamma_t\) be a curve shortening flow. Suppose that the rescaled solution \(\Lambda \Gamma_{t / \Lambda^2}\) converges to a straight line. By multiplicity one conjecture, if \(\Lambda \gg 1\), \(\Theta (\Lambda \Gamma_{t/ \Lambda^2} , 0 , 1) \approx 1\). Then, \(\Lambda \Gamma_{t/\Lambda^2}\) has \(\kappa \le C\), which is a contradiction. Therefore, a straight line cannot be our solution.

docs.title: 3.2 Huisken's Distance Comparison Principle
docs.text:
Theorem 3.2.1 (Huisken distance comparison)3. For a curve shortening flow \(\Gamma_t\), \(t \ge 0\), define

\[ l(x,y,t) = l_t (\gamma(x,t) , \gamma (y,t) ), \quad d(x,y,t) = |\gamma(x,t) - \gamma(y,t)| \]

where \(l_t\) is the intrinsic distance. Also, define

\[ R(t) = \sup_{\begin{smallmatrix} x \ne y\\ x,y\in S^1 \end{smallmatrix}} \frac{L(t)}{\pi d(x,y,t)} \cdot \sin \left (\frac{\pi l(x,y,t)}{L(t)} \right ). \]

Then, \(R(t)\) is monotone decreasing.

Because this functional \(R(t)\) is bounded entirely by its initial geometry at \(t=0\), it immediately grants us a uniform upper bound on the ratio of intrinsic to extrinsic distance across the evolving curve.

Remark. Then, we can bound \(l/d\):

\[ \frac{l}{d} = \underbrace{\frac{L}{\pi d} \sin \left ( \frac{\pi l}{L} \right )}_{\le R(0)} \cdot \frac{\frac{l \pi}{L}}{\sin \left ( \frac{\pi l}{L} \right )} \le C \cdot R(0). \]

Note that \(\frac{L}{\pi d} \sin \left ( \frac{\pi l}{L} \right )\) is bounded by Theorem 3.2.1.

docs.title: 3.3 Type I and Type II Singularities
docs.text:
Lemma 3.3.1.

\[ \frac{d}{dt} \int_{\Gamma_t} |\kappa| \, ds = -2 \sum_{\{x \mid \kappa(x,t) = 0\}} |\kappa_s(x,t)| \]

where the set of zeroes is finite, or \(\kappa \equiv 0\). Consequently, the limit

\[ \lim_{t \nearrow T (=t_0)} \int_{\Gamma_t} |\kappa| \, ds \]

exists.

The fact that this total absolute curvature integral remains definitively bounded as we approach the singular time provides the key analytical constraint needed to rule out rapidly forming singularities.

Proof of Theorem that singularities are Type I. Suppose not. That is, assume

\[ \sup_{t < T} \sqrt{T-t} \max_{\Gamma_t} |\kappa| = \infty. \]

For all \(k \in \mathbb{N}\), choose \((y_k, t_k)\) such that it achieves the maximum for

\[ \max_{t \in \left[0, T - \frac{1}{k}\right]} \max_{\Gamma_t} \left( T - \frac{1}{k} - t \right) \cdot \kappa^2. \]

Denote \(\kappa(y_k, t_k) := \lambda_k\). (This is an application of Hamilton's point-picking method4).

We then define the parabolically rescaled flow:

\[ \tilde{\Gamma}_t^i = \lambda_i \left( \Gamma_{t_i + \frac{t}{\lambda_i^2}} - y_i \right). \]

Then, because of the bounds established by the point-picking method, we can extract a smoothly converging limit sequence as \(i \to \infty\):

\[ \tilde{\Gamma}_t^i \longrightarrow \Gamma_t^\infty \quad \text{for} \quad -\infty < t < +\infty. \]

This limit flow \(\Gamma_t^\infty\) is an eternal solution, and it inherently satisfies the following curvature properties:

\[ |\kappa^\infty| \le 1 \quad \text{everywhere, and} \quad |\kappa^\infty(0,0)| = 1. \]

Claim: The limit flow \(\Gamma_t^\infty\) is convex, meaning \(\kappa^\infty > 0\).

Assuming the claim that \(\Gamma_t^\infty\) is strictly convex (\(\kappa^\infty > 0\)), we can now completely classify this limit flow. By our parabolic rescaling construction, \(\Gamma_t^\infty\) is an eternal solution (meaning it exists for \(t \in (-\infty, \infty)\)) that attains its global maximum curvature \(\kappa^\infty(0,0) = 1\).

The only completely convex, eternal solutions to the curve shortening flow in the plane are the shrinking circle and the translating Grim Reaper. However, a shrinking circle collapses to a point in finite time, meaning it cannot exist for all \(t \in \mathbb{R}\). Therefore, the limit \(\Gamma_t^\infty\) must be the Grim Reaper.

A Grim Reaper with a maximum curvature of \(1\) translates along an axis and is asymptotically bounded by two parallel lines separated by an extrinsic distance of \(d = \pi\).

Suppose we pick two points on the opposite asymptotic branches of the Grim Reaper. Their extrinsic spatial distance in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), denoted as \(d\), is strictly bounded by \(\pi\). However, the intrinsic distance along the curve between these two points, denoted as \(l\), approaches \(\infty\). Thus, on the limit curve \(\Gamma_t^\infty\), the chord-arc ratio is unbounded:

\[ \frac{l}{d} \longrightarrow \infty. \]

This brings us to the fundamental contradiction. For the original simple closed curve \(\Gamma_t\), Theorem 3.2.1 guarantees that the chord-arc ratio (intrinsic distance over extrinsic distance) is uniformly bounded by some constant \(C\) for all \(t < T\):

\[ \frac{l}{d} < C. \]

Because this geometric ratio is perfectly invariant under parabolic rescaling, the rescaled sequence \(\tilde{\Gamma}_t^i\) must also obey \(\frac{l}{d} < C\). Since \(\tilde{\Gamma}_t^i\) converges smoothly (with multiplicity 1) to the Grim Reaper, the limit Grim Reaper must also satisfy this bound, which we have shown is impossible.

Therefore, our initial assumption that the singularity is Type II is false. We conclude that all singularities for embedded curves under curve shortening flow must be Type I. \(\blacksquare\)

To finalize the classification of this limit geometry, we must verify the claim that the eternal limit flow is indeed completely convex.

Proof of claim. We want to show that the eternal limit flow \(\Gamma_t^\infty\) is strictly convex (\(\kappa^\infty > 0\)).

Fix an arbitrary time interval \([a, b]\) with \(-\infty < a < b < \infty\). Using the lemma we established earlier for the evolution of the total absolute curvature, we integrate this quantity over the given time interval for our rescaled sequence \(\tilde{\Gamma}_t^i\). Note that the time \(t\) in the rescaled flow corresponds to \(t_i + \frac{t}{\lambda_i^2}\) in the original flow. By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus:

\[ -2 \int_a^b \sum_{\{x \mid \tilde{\kappa}_i(x,t) = 0\}} |(\tilde{\kappa}_i)_s| \, dt = \left[ \int_{\Gamma_t} |\kappa| \, ds \right]_{t = t_i + \frac{b}{\lambda_i^2}} - \left[ \int_{\Gamma_t} |\kappa| \, ds \right]_{t = t_i + \frac{a}{\lambda_i^2}}. \]

As established in our lemma, \(\int_{\Gamma_t} |\kappa| \, ds\) is monotonically decreasing and bounded strictly below, meaning its limit as \(t \nearrow T\) absolutely exists. As \(i \to \infty\), we know that \(t_i \to T\) and \(\lambda_i \to \infty\). Consequently, both time evaluations on the right-hand side converge to the singular time \(T\). Therefore, the difference between these integrals must vanish:

\[ \lim_{i \to \infty} \left( \left[ \int_{\Gamma_t} |\kappa| \, ds \right]_{t = t_i + \frac{b}{\lambda_i^2}} - \left[ \int_{\Gamma_t} |\kappa| \, ds \right]_{t = t_i + \frac{a}{\lambda_i^2}} \right) = 0. \]

Taking \(i \to \infty\) for the left-hand side yields the behavior of the limit flow \(\Gamma_t^\infty\). Extending our arbitrary interval \([a, b]\) to the entire real line \((-\infty, \infty)\), we obtain:

\[ \int_{-\infty}^\infty \sum_{\{x \mid \kappa^\infty(x,t) = 0\}} |\kappa^\infty_s| \, dt = 0. \]

Because the integrand is strictly non-negative, this integral evaluating to zero implies a strong geometric constraint: at any spacetime point where the limit curvature vanishes (\(\kappa^\infty = 0\)), its spatial derivative must also vanish (\(\kappa^\infty_s = 0\)).

Graphically, if \(\kappa^\infty\) were to change sign (crossing the \(s\)-axis), it would exhibit a non-zero derivative at the root, which we have just proven is impossible. Thus, if the curvature graph ever touches \(0\), it must be perfectly tangent to the axis. By the strong maximum principle for the curvature evolution equation \(\kappa_t = \kappa_{ss} + \kappa^3\), if \(\kappa^\infty = 0\) and \(\kappa^\infty_s = 0\) at any point, then the curvature must be identically zero (\(\kappa^\infty \equiv 0\)) everywhere.

However, our blow-up sequence construction guarantees that the maximum curvature is preserved at the origin, specifically \(|\kappa^\infty(0,0)| = 1\). This means \(\kappa^\infty\) cannot be identically zero. Since it cannot be identically zero and it cannot cross the axis, it must be strictly positive or strictly negative everywhere. By our standard inward-pointing orientation convention for closed curves, we conclude that \(\kappa^\infty > 0\).

Hence, the limit flow \(\Gamma_t^\infty\) is strictly convex. \(\blacksquare\)

  1. White, B. (2005). A local regularity theorem for mean curvature flow. Annals of Mathematics, 161, 1487-1519. ↩

  2. Perelman, G. (2002). The entropy formula for the Ricci flow and its geometric applications. arXiv preprint math/0211159. ↩

  3. Huisken, G. (1998). A distance comparison principle for evolving curves. Asian Journal of Mathematics, 2, 127-133. ↩

  4. Hamilton, R. S. (1995). The formation of singularities in the Ricci flow. Surveys in Differential Geometry, Vol. II, 7-136. ↩

docs.title: 4.1 Summary of Lecture
docs.text:
Throughout this lecture, we have rigorously built the machinery required to understand the macroscopic and microscopic behavior of the curve shortening flow. By analyzing the evolution of intrinsic geometric quantities, we saw that any simple closed curve must inevitably develop a singularity in finite time, as its enclosed area decreases at a strictly constant rate of \(2\pi\).

The crux of our analysis lay in classifying the precise nature of this final singularity. By leveraging parabolic rescaling, Gaussian density, and Hamilton's point-picking method, we extracted eternal limit flows. Then, using Huisken's distance comparison principle, we generated a geometric contradiction that systematically ruled out the Grim Reaper, proving that Type II singularities cannot form on simple closed curves.

This powerful restriction forces all singularities for embedded curves to be Type I. Because the only compact, embedded Type I singularity model in the plane is the shrinking circle, the curve's ultimate fate is geometrically sealed:

  • Grayson's Phase: Any initial "dents" or regions of negative curvature are pushed outward and smoothed out faster than the overall curve collapses. The avoidance principle and the exclusion of Type II singular bottlenecks guarantee that the curve becomes strictly convex without ever self-intersecting.
  • Gage-Hamilton's Phase: Once the curve is strictly convex, the flow acts as a perfectly symmetric heat equation, driving the geometry toward perfect isotropy. The curve asymptotically rounds into a perfect circle as it shrinks down to a single singular point.

This completes the modern PDE-based perspective on the Gage-Hamilton-Grayson Theorem. Ultimately, the curve shortening flow serves as a beautiful, mathematically rich paradigm for parabolic geometric flows. The techniques developed here—maximum principles, monotonicity formulas, and blow-up analysis—lay the essential conceptual groundwork for studying higher-dimensional flows, such as the Mean Curvature Flow and the Ricci Flow, which dictate the topology of the universe itself.

docs.title: 4.2 Generalizations: Mean Curvature and Ricci Flow
docs.text: While the curve shortening flow provides a profound geometric framework for 1-dimensional curves in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), its underlying principles naturally generalize to higher dimensions and intrinsic geometries.

docs.title: 4.2.1 Mean Curvature Flow (Extrinsic)
docs.text:
The most direct higher-dimensional analog to the curve shortening flow is the Mean Curvature Flow (MCF). Instead of a curve, we consider an \(n\)-dimensional hypersurface \(M_t\) embedded in \(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\). The flow equation is governed by:

\[ \partial_t x = \vec{H} \]

where \(\vec{H}\) is the mean curvature vector. While Huisken proved that strictly convex surfaces under MCF shrink to round points (analogous to the Gage-Hamilton phase), Grayson's theorem does not hold in higher dimensions. Non-convex surfaces can develop localized singularities before collapsing entirely, such as the famous "neckpinch" singularity (e.g., a topological dumbbell snapping in the middle).

docs.title: 4.2.2 Ricci Flow (Intrinsic)
docs.text:
Rather than embedding a manifold in a higher-dimensional ambient space, one can evolve the intrinsic geometry of the manifold itself. This is achieved by the Ricci flow, introduced by Richard Hamilton in 19821. For a Riemannian manifold equipped with a metric tensor \(g_{ij}\), the Ricci flow is defined by the evolution equation:

\[ \partial_t g_{ij} = -2R_{ij} \]

where \(R_{ij}\) is the Ricci curvature tensor. This equation acts as a non-linear diffusion equation for the metric. In the rigorous theoretical frameworks of General Relativity, the vacuum Einstein field equations demand that the Ricci tensor vanishes (\(R_{ij} = 0\)). In this context, the Ricci flow can be viewed as a dynamical, parabolic system seeking to smooth the metric toward such an exact Einstein manifold.

docs.title: 4.2.3 Perelman's Monotonicity and the Poincaré Conjecture
docs.text:
Hamilton introduced the Ricci flow with the ambitious goal of proving Thurston's Geometrization Conjecture, which contains the famous Poincaré Conjecture as a special case1. However, much like the neckpinches in the Mean Curvature Flow, the Ricci flow develops severe, complex singularities in 3 dimensions that halt the flow.

The critical breakthrough came in 2002 when Grisha Perelman introduced a deeply physics-inspired functional called the \(\mathcal{W}\)-entropy2. He proved a remarkable monotonicity formula, establishing that this entropy is strictly non-decreasing along the Ricci flow:

\[ \frac{d}{dt} \mathcal{W}(g_{ij}, f, \tau) \ge 0 \]

This monotonicity was revolutionary. It definitively ruled out the existence of "breather" singularities (regions of spacetime that fluctuate wildly without resolving) and provided the strict analytic control needed to classify all local singularity models (the "point selection argument" utilized earlier in these notes originates from this exact paper). By meticulously performing geometric surgery to cut out these singularities before they could disrupt the flow, Perelman pushed the Ricci flow to its topological limit, successfully resolving the Poincaré Conjecture.

  1. Hamilton, R. S. (1982). Three-manifolds with positive Ricci curvature. Journal of Differential Geometry, 17(2), 255-306. ↩↩

  2. Perelman, G. (2002). The entropy formula for the Ricci flow and its geometric applications. arXiv preprint math/0211159. ↩
